definition: Two names given to Spinoza's doctrine by his readers. Pantheism identifies God and the world: everything is in God, and God is nothing outside nature; this is how the pantheism controversy, opened by Jacobi in 1785, and the Romantics read the Ethics, some to denounce it as disguised atheism, others to find in it a religion of the universe, like Schleiermacher hailing Spinoza as holy and outcast. Hegel reverses the reading in his lectures on the history of philosophy: Spinozism is not an atheism but an acosmism; there is not too little God in Spinoza, but too much, since the finite world loses all reality of its own. The essay concludes that these two opposite readings say the same thing: Spinoza did not do away with God, he displaced him. The word pantheism returns in Part Six, where the King of Prussia brings Schelling to Berlin to combat the dragon's seed of Hegelian pantheism, and where the young Feuerbach is still a pantheist of the spirit. See also Deus seu Natura, Intellectual love of God, Deism.

Pierre Bayle's hypothesis in the Pensées diverses sur la comète (1682-1683): a society of atheists could subsist and govern itself as well as a society of pagans, provided crimes were severely punished. Bayle starts from an observation: people do not live according to their principles; convinced Christians commit every sin, and it is human justice that makes the greater part of the world virtuous. Religion is therefore not the cement of morality, and atheism is no worse than idolatry, for which Jurieu will reproach him in an attested response. The essay sees in it the first exit from religion as a political bond, from a sceptical Calvinist, and the first of the five answers in the constructed debate on morality without God: morality holds through society. It sets it against Ivan Karamazov: Bayle speaks of society, Ivan of conscience; a society of atheists can hold together with laws and prisons, but Smerdyakov's crime raises another question, that of guilt. Young Kolya, in the novel, states Bayle's thesis as a schoolboy would. See also Everything is permitted, Civil religion, Theodicy.

The thesis of the Theodicy (1710): God, being perfect, chose among all possible worlds the one that contains the most perfection, and the evil it contains, the metaphysical evil of finitude, the physical evil of suffering, the moral evil of sin, is the condition of a greater good in the whole. Leibniz thus answers Bayle, who held the problem of evil to be insoluble by reason, in an attested response. Voltaire turns the formula round after the Lisbon earthquake (1755): Candide (1759) has Pangloss repeat that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds, and ends on the garden to be cultivated. The essay judges that theodicy accepts the sacrifice of the individual to harmony and asks each person to sacrifice their complaint; it sees in it the distant origin of the revolt of Ivan Karamazov, who refuses harmony out of love for humanity and returns his ticket, in a constructed confrontation. Leibniz's question about the existence of the world nevertheless survives his answer. See also Theodicy, Principle of sufficient reason, Everything is permitted.

The great principle, not commonly used, that Leibniz formulates in § 7 of the Principles of Nature and Grace (1714): nothing happens without a sufficient reason, that is, without its being possible for someone who knew things well enough to give a reason why it is so and not otherwise. The Monadology (§ 32) sets it beside the principle of contradiction. Applied to the totality of things, it gives rise to the question the essay places at the centre of its last constructed debate: why is there something rather than nothing, since nothing is simpler and easier than something? Since no contingent thing accounts for the whole series, the ultimate reason of things must lie in a necessary substance, God. The essay follows the fate of this demand: Hume dissolves it, Kant sees in it the abyss of reason, Schelling drives it to despair, Heidegger turns it against Leibniz, Wittgenstein keeps the wonder without the answer. It notes that the demand for reason leads to piety by a back door, and that it is when wonder becomes debt that spirituality becomes religion again. See also Wonder without debt, Best of all possible worlds, Causa sui.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the religion that reason could establish by itself, without revelation: the existence of a God, author of the world, known through the order of nature, and the duties that follow from it. The deists saw it as the common ground of all religions; the apologists, as a preparation for faith. Hume tests it from both sides. The Natural History of Religion (1757) replaces the question of foundation with that of origin: religion is born of fear and hope, polytheism precedes monotheism, and the whole remains a riddle. The Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779) have three characters discuss the argument from design, and Philo, the sceptic, ruins its force while leaving the twelfth part ambiguous. Rousseau proposes another version in the Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar: a natural religion that is not that of the philosophers, founded on inner feeling rather than demonstration, which Kant will take up while acknowledging his debt. The essay notes that Hume alone, among the Enlightenment thinkers, puts no capitalized word in the place of God. See also Deism, Eight regimes of critique, Feeling of absolute dependence.

False worship. The fourth part of Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason (1793), the most violent, deals with service and false service under the dominion of the good principle, or with religion and priestcraft. Kant lays down there a principle he declares self-evident: whatever, apart from a good way of life, the human being supposes he can still do to become well-pleasing to God is mere religious delusion and false service of God. Prayers, pilgrimages, fasts, rites and sacraments, taken as means of winning God's favour, belong to fetishism, and the Church that lives off them is priestcraft. The essay measures the reach of this text by a Lutheran raised in pietism, which turns almost all actual religious practice into fetishism, and finds in it the name of religion without spirituality: observance, worship that commits the one who performs it to no transformation. It also notes that Kant, by reducing religion to the recognition of our duties as divine commands, sacralized morality, for which Nietzsche will reproach him in The Antichrist as an underhand theology. See also Spirituality, Fetishism, Religio, relegere, religare.

Intuition and feeling. In On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers (1799), Schleiermacher defines the essence of religion against the two reductions of his century: it is neither thinking nor acting, but intuition and feeling, sense and taste for the infinite, “Sinn und Geschmack fürs Unendliche”. Kant had reduced it to morality, rationalist metaphysics to the proofs of God; Schleiermacher places it in the immediate experience of the universe, prior to all dogma and every Church, to the point that a religion without God can be better than a religion with a badly conceived God. The essay sees in it the birth of the regime of experience and the first attempt to leave instituted religion without leaving lived religion. It also marks its structural weakness, which will hold for James, Otto and Bergson: experience proves that one feels, it does not prove what one feels. Hegel will answer that if religion were a feeling of dependence, the dog would be the best Christian; Feuerbach will answer in 1851 that the dependence felt is dependence on nature, and Barth will say in 1927 that Feuerbach is the truth of Schleiermacher. See also Feeling of absolute dependence, Eight regimes of critique, Numinous.

The formula that closes Faith and Knowledge (1802). There Hegel cites the feeling on which the religion of modern times rests, that God himself is dead, “Gott selbst ist tot”, drawing on Pascal's words about a nature that everywhere marks a lost God. Philosophy must restore this historical Good Friday as a speculative Good Friday, in the whole truth and harshness of its godlessness, so that the highest totality may rise again in the most serene freedom of its shape. The death of God is thus thought as a moment of the concept: the finite is traversed and negated, the absolute passes through negation. The essay specifies that the hymn by Johann Rist, from which the sentence comes, is brought in only later, in the Lectures, and that Nietzsche will keep this death of God while taking away the resurrection. It holds Hegel's argument to be right and his conclusion wrong: philosophy, which sublates religion into the concept, becomes the higher religion of the wise, one more Averroist division. See also Death of God, Aufhebung, Onto-theology.

The cultivated philistine. Nietzsche coins the word in the first of his Untimely Meditations, David Strauss, the Confessor and the Writer (1873), against the author of The Old Faith and the New (1872). Strauss, whose Life of Jesus of 1835 had ruined the imposture thesis by showing that the gospel narratives were myths formed without intent to deceive, proposes forty years later a new faith, a piety towards the universe nourished by science, by Beethoven and Haydn, and by common morality. Nietzsche reproaches him not with being too critical but with not being critical enough: he has done away with the Christian God and kept Christian morality intact, without seeing that the one does not stand without the other, and he is content with this half-measure with the good conscience of the man of letters. The essay ranks this attested response among the first applications of the law of refoundations, and links the cultivated philistine with the atheists of the marketplace of The Gay Science: in both cases the absence of God is taken as a settled matter whose consequences have not been measured. See also Atheists of the marketplace, Law of refoundations, Death of God.

The genus, the human species conceived as essence. For Feuerbach the individual is finite, but the species is infinite: reason, will and heart, which make up the essence of man, have their limit in no individual and are realized in humanity as a whole. God is nothing but this essence of the species, separated from the individual and worshipped as a being apart: the consciousness of God is the self-consciousness of man, and the secret of theology is anthropology. The essay shows that the operation had already been carried out by David Friedrich Strauss in 1835: the predicates the Church attributes to Christ contradict one another in an individual and agree in the idea of the species; humanity is God made man. Stirner turns the argument round: Man, the species, is one more alienation, a ghost that demands of the individual the same sacrifice as God. Marx reproaches Feuerbach, in the sixth thesis, with making the human essence an abstraction inherent in the isolated individual, whereas it is the ensemble of social relations. See also Projection, Homo homini Deus, Spuk.

Man is a God to man. The formula, turned round from Hobbes's saying that man is a wolf to man, concludes Feuerbach's critique: if the essence of man is man's supreme being, the first law must be the love of man for man. Feuerbach makes it the supreme practical principle and the turning point of world history; in the Principles of the Philosophy of the Future (1843) he writes that the unity of I and Thou is God, and that human relations, love, friendship, are in themselves truly religious. The essay reads in it the moment when critique turns into consecration: Feuerbach gives up the name of God and keeps the thing, worship, by transferring it to the whole of man. This is the textbook case of soft refoundation and the target of the reproach Engels made in 1886, when he saw in this love a magician god and in this philosophy a religion that Feuerbach wanted to complete rather than abolish. Stirner had said the same as early as 1844: the fear of Man is only a modified form of the fear of God. See also Gattung, Strict refoundation and soft refoundation, Pious atheists.

The ghost, the haunting. In The Ego and Its Own (1844), Stirner gives this name to every authority one places above oneself and to which one must sacrifice oneself: God, but also Man, Humanity, the State, Truth, Morality, Freedom. Feuerbach had shown that God was the alienated human essence; Stirner shows that the human essence is itself an alienation, and that whoever believes in it has a screw loose. Political liberalism, socialism and the humanism of Feuerbach and Bauer are for him stages of this haunting, theological insurrections that change masters without changing the relation: our atheists are pious people. The essay makes this analysis the very formulation of the law of refoundations, and observes that Stirner does not escape it, since the Unique One, who has set his cause on nothing, settles into the place left empty just as God did, as Nietzsche will object to him. Marx, in The German Ideology, answers Saint Max that his isolated individual is only an abstraction. See also Pious atheists, Law of refoundations, Gattung.

The sentence of Stirner's that the essay takes as its guiding thread: “Unsere Atheisten sind fromme Leute”, our atheists are pious people. It targets the Young Hegelians, and Feuerbach first of all: they have dismissed God but kept the sacred, by transferring it to Man, and the fear of Man is only a modified form of the fear of God; in the feudal age everything was held in fief from God, in the liberal age everything is held from Man. Feuerbach turns the phrase back on him in an attested response of 1845: Stirner too is a pious atheist, who worships his Ego. The essay judges the retort right about Stirner and weak about the rest, and retains the formula as the law of the whole series, which its author stated without escaping it. It recurs even among contemporaries: Onfray, according to a reported formula, accuses Comte-Sponville of being a Christian atheist, that is, a pious atheist who keeps Christian morality and abandons only God, before becoming one himself, differently, by defending the Latin Mass. See also Law of refoundations, Spuk, Christian atheist.

The word comes from Charles de Brosses, Du culte des dieux fétiches (1760), who uses it for the worship of material objects held to be powers, and whom Tylor quotes as an epigraph to Primitive Culture. It has two critical uses in the essay. Kant, in 1793, applies the vocabulary of the fetish to Christian worship: every rite performed to win God's favour is fetish worship, a false service. Marx, a reader of de Brosses, takes it up in the first volume of Capital (1867) to speak of the commodity: in exchange, the relations between people take on the fantastic form of relations between things, and the products of labour seem endowed with a life of their own; to understand this fetishism, he says, one must take flight into the misty region of the religious world. The critique of religion thus becomes the model for the critique of economics. The essay notes that Marx describes there the cult of abstract man, the religion proper to commodity society, and that the emancipation he promises, a transparent society delivered from its fetishes, inherits the function of salvation. See also Opium of the people, Afterdienst, Projection.

The word Marx uses, in the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right (1844), just before the sentence on opium: religious distress is at once the expression of real distress and the protest against real distress, “die Protestation gegen das wirkliche Elend”; religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, the spirit of a spiritless age. The essay writes the word with a capital letter to make a concept of it: religion is not only an illusory consolation, it is also a complaint, and the critique that wants to abolish religion must demand that one give up a condition that needs illusions. It is through the Protestation that Marx remains right against the sages of immanence: Comte-Sponville's oceanic experience consoles, it does not protest; Spinoza, faced with Ivan Karamazov, does not answer the complaint. The conclusion seeks to hold together Spinoza's acceptance and Marx's Protestation, by consenting to the necessity of the world without consenting to the injustice of men. See also Opium of the people, Sigh without a heaven, Revolt.

The doctrine of the Course of Positive Philosophy (1830-1842): the human mind passes through the theological state, in which it explains phenomena by supernatural wills, fetishes, gods or a single God; through the metaphysical state, in which it explains them by abstract entities, Nature, forces, essences; and finally through the positive state, in which it gives up seeking causes in order to establish laws between phenomena. Each science passes through these states at its own pace, and sociology, the last to be born, completes the cycle. The essay stresses what follows, less often read: after the subjective turn linked to Clotilde de Vaux, Comte founds a complete religion of Humanity, with dogma, worship and priesthood, and this foundation is not a late madness but the logical consequence of the three states, since one must regulate and rally, and one destroys only what one replaces. Löwith recognizes in it a history of salvation in three ages, heir to Joachim of Fiore's division of history into the ages of the Father, the Son and the Spirit. See also Great Being, Religion of Humanity, Secularized eschatology.

The object of the positivist religion, named in the Catechism of Positive Religion (1852): Comte condenses the whole of positive conceptions into the single notion of an immense and eternal being, Humanity. The Great Being is the whole of past, future and present beings who freely concur in perfecting the universal order; it is composed first of all of the dead, the living being more and more governed by them, and it directly inspires the sacred formula of positivism: Love as principle, Order as basis, and Progress as end. Around it are organized a dogma, a worship, sacraments, a calendar and a priesthood. The essay notes that Comte founds something sacred and makes no secret of it, and that the catechumen of the dialogue, by confessing her personal nullity before the Great Being, herself formulates Stirner's objection. Durkheim will reproach him with wanting to revive artificially a religion that social life has not produced. The Great Being figures among the strict refoundations of the conclusion; the essay sees in it the proof by fact of what Stirner asserted by argument. See also Law of the three stages, Religion of Humanity, Strict refoundation and soft refoundation.

In the strict sense, the religion founded by Auguste Comte after 1847, of which the Catechism of Positive Religion (1852) gives the summary exposition: a religion without God, whose object is the Great Being, Humanity, with its temples, among them the one in the rue Payenne in Paris and those of Brazil, where the motto Ordem e Progresso passed onto the flag. In the broad sense, the essay uses the phrase for every exit from religion that transfers the divine onto humanity: the one Strauss begins by making humanity God made man, the one Feuerbach theorizes, the one George Eliot, translator of both, puts into novels, the one Luc Ferry renews under the name of the divinization of the human. The Grand Inquisitor is its political completion: a religion of humanity administered by those who know, the essay speaking of a Comte become lucid, and therefore tragic. The question the essay puts to each of these forms is the same: does Humanity thus consecrated demand that one sacrifice to it? In Comte the answer is yes, and the refoundation is strict. See also Great Being, Gattung, Homo homini Deus.

Wille zum Leben. In The World as Will and Representation (1819), Schopenhauer gives this name to the thing in itself: beneath representations, a blind willing, without aim and without rest, which objectifies itself in all beings and whose law is suffering, since every desire arises from a lack and every satisfaction opens another. Deliverance can come only from the denial of this willing, through aesthetic contemplation, provisionally, then through asceticism and compassion, which recognize the suffering of all that lives. Schopenhauer calls this denial holiness and redemption, recognizes himself in Eckhart and in the sages of India, and concludes that this world, so real, with all its suns, is nothing. The essay draws from this that Schopenhauer left God without leaving the religion of salvation, and that he is the first to read the mystics and Buddhism outside any theology. Nietzsche breaks with him on this point: pity is the practice of nihilism, and the denial of the will to live the subtlest survival of Christianity. See also Nihilism, Nirvana, Gelassenheit.

The formula attributed to Ivan Karamazov: if God does not exist, everything is permitted. The essay shows that it never appears in this proverbial form in The Brothers Karamazov. It is Rakitin who reports Ivan's thesis, without the immortality of the soul there is no virtue and everything is permitted, and Ivan, when questioned, answers only that he will not renounce the formula. Sartre, in Existentialism Is a Humanism, attributes to him the sentence fabricated by the reception, “Si Dieu n'existait pas, tout serait permis”, if God did not exist, everything would be permitted, and turns it into the task of freedom; Camus, in The Rebel, makes the history of contemporary nihilism begin with this everything is permitted. The essay reads in Ivan's thesis Voltaire's answer reversed: if God is necessary to morality and God does not exist, morality collapses. It sets it against Bayle, for whom a society of atheists can hold together: Bayle speaks of society, Ivan of conscience, and Smerdyakov's crime, which takes Ivan at his word, shows that the question is not one of order but of guilt. See also Society of atheists, Grand Inquisitor, Nihilism.

Wille zur Wahrheit. § 344 of The Gay Science, entitled in what sense we too are still pious, holds that the demand on which science rests is not itself scientific: it is a faith, and Nietzsche admits that today's godless still take their fire from the blaze that a thousand-year-old faith kindled, the faith that God is truth. The third essay of On the Genealogy of Morality (§ 24-27) goes further: the ascetic ideal has dominated all philosophy because truth was posited there as being, as God, as supreme authority; honest atheism is the last form of this ideal, which ends by forbidding itself the lie of belief in God and abolishes itself. The essay makes this paragraph the key to the Nietzschean exception: Nietzsche escapes Stirner's law because he knows where his fire comes from. It also turns § 344 against Freud, who held that our science is not an illusion, and recalls that Nietzsche, asking what truth does to the one who seeks it, recovers against the Cartesian moment the question of spirituality. See also Ascetic ideal, Genealogy, Death of God.

The subject of the third essay of On the Genealogy of Morality (1887): what do ascetic ideals mean? In the priest, asceticism is the means by which suffering life turns against itself in order to last; it gives suffering a meaning, guilt, and this meaning, however terrible, is better than meaninglessness, for man would rather will nothingness than not will. § 24 to 28 extend the diagnosis to science and atheism: the unconditional will to truth is the most recent and noblest form of the ascetic ideal, and it is Christian morality itself, truthfulness raised into a duty, that triumphed over the Christian God. The essay reads in it both an anticipation of the theories of secularization, Weber and Gauchet rediscovering this self-abolition of the religious by the religious, and the objection Nietzsche addresses in advance to Simone Weil, whose refusal of consolation resembles an asceticism; the essay judges it partly right, while noting that Weil refuses to give misfortune a meaning. See also Will to truth, Genealogy, Disenchantment of the world.

The French word that Nietzsche keeps as it is in the German text of the first essay of On the Genealogy of Morality (1887) to name the mainspring of slave morality: the imaginary revenge of those who cannot act, who overturn the values of the masters and call good what is weak, humble and suffering. Christianity is for him its major work, and Paul, in The Antichrist, its inventor; Jesus, by contrast, is in The Antichrist a being incapable of resistance, of ressentiment and of dogma, who lives in an inner kingdom, and the essay links this portrait with the silent Christ of the Grand Inquisitor. The essay places ressentiment among the genealogies to which William James replies in advance: Feuerbach explained religion by projection, Marx by misery, Nietzsche by ressentiment, Freud by infantile desire, and to all of them James objects that a tree is judged by its fruits, not by its roots. See also Genealogy, Nihilism, Overman.

Übermensch. The figure Zarathustra announces: man is something that must be overcome, and the overman is the meaning of the earth, the one who, after the death of God, creates his own values instead of receiving them. The essay does not make the overman the centre of its reading of Nietzsche, which it seeks rather in The Gay Science and the Genealogy, but it meets him in the objections. The first is the one Dostoevsky might have formulated: are amor fati and the overman not figures of Kirillov, the man who makes himself god because there is no God, and Zarathustra, with his disciples and his parables, one more religion? Nietzsche himself feared it, writing that there was nothing in him of a founder of religion and that he wanted no believers. The second comes from Bergson, who answers that the overman already exists and is called the mystic, in whom open morality and dynamic religion have found their man. The essay holds Nietzsche to be an exception, but one of attitude, unstable: § 344 against the prophetic temptations of Zarathustra. See also Amor fati, Death of God, Static religion and dynamic religion.

In Durkheim, the state of exaltation produced by the gathering of a group, in the ceremonies of the Australian Aborigines as in the nights of the French Revolution, from which the sacred is born: the assembled individuals feel a force that surpasses them and refer it to an external being, totem, god, Fatherland or Reason, which is only society itself hypostatized. It is through effervescence that a living cult can be born, and that is why Durkheim reproaches Comte with having wanted to revive a religion artificially: from life itself, and not from a dead past, a living cult can arise; a day will come when our societies will again know hours of creative effervescence, and there are no immortal gospels. The essay sees in it one of the two strongest objections to its thesis, and the most disturbing, since the political religions of the twentieth century are that very effervescence. The essay sets Weber against it: the gods have already returned, but in the plural and without restoring unity; and Malinowski, for whom the effervescence of crowds is often entirely profane. See also The sacred, Collective representations, Secular religions.

The notion on which Durkheim founds the sociology of religion. The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912) opens with the thesis that religion is an eminently social thing: religious representations are collective representations that express collective realities, and rites are ways of acting that arise within assembled groups. The very categories of thought, time, space, cause, totality, would have a religious, and therefore social, origin. It follows that there are no false religions: all answer, in their own way, to the given conditions of human existence, and the god is only the figurative expression of society. The essay sees in it Feuerbach transposed from the human species to the group, but with the opposite conclusion, since projection, far from being an error to be dispelled, is the condition of all common life. Bergson readily admits the existence of collective representations deposited in institutions, language and customs, but refuses to make society the sole source of the sacred: it is only one source of it, and the lowest. See also The sacred, Collective effervescence, Projection.

Stahlhartes Gehäuse, the image that closes The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1904-1905, revised in 1920). The Puritan wanted to work in a calling; we are compelled to. Concern for external goods was to lie on the shoulders of the saint like a light cloak, but fate turned the cloak into a casing as hard as steel, and asceticism, leaving the monks' cells for working life, built the cosmos of the modern economy, which now holds without its religious mainspring. For the last men of this development Weber envisages specialists without spirit and sensualists without heart, who imagine they have reached a level of humanity never before attained. The translation as iron cage comes from Talcott Parsons; the essay says casing. It reads this page as the Weberian version of the self-abolition of the religious by the religious: Protestant asceticism produced a world that no longer needs it, as in Nietzsche Christian truthfulness killed the Christian God. See also Disenchantment of the world, Polytheism of values, Sacrifice of the intellect.

The diagnosis of Science as a Vocation (1917-1919): the many old gods, disenchanted and become impersonal powers, rise from their graves and resume their eternal struggle. The disenchanted world is not a world without gods, but a world in which the ultimate standpoints on life, the true, the beautiful, the sacred, the nation, are irreducible to one another and no science can decide between them; each must choose his god, and science says only at what price. The essay marks the difference from Durkheim: Durkheim expected new gods born of an effervescence that would restore the unity of society; Weber observes that the gods have returned in the plural and will restore no unity. The exit from monotheism is not an exit from religion but a return to polytheism, without temples or sacrifices but not without victims, and the essay's thesis takes on a new form: one does not refound a religion, one refounds several, which wage war on one another. Weber offers no consolation and refuses the prophets of the lecture hall. See also Disenchantment of the world, Casing as hard as steel, Sacrifice of the intellect.

Opfer des Intellekts, the formula of Science as a Vocation. Whoever cannot bear the fate of the age, a world without mysterious and incalculable powers, where the prophets fall silent, may return to the arms of the old Churches, wide open and full of mercy; Weber says he must do so simply, without fuss, and that this return demands of him the sacrifice of the intellect, the acceptance of believing what reason cannot establish. He does not despise it: the sacrifice of the intellect for the sake of a positive faith is morally better than the false reconciliation of those who dare not choose; Weber does, however, refuse the prophets of the lecture hall. The expression comes from the Catholic tradition, where the sacrificium intellectus designates the submission of reason to dogma. The essay acknowledges the probity of this position, which refuses both to found a cult and to pass off a value as knowledge, and judges it hard to hold; it wonders whether Weber, who ends on the watchman of Edom and the night that lasts, might not be the last Puritan. See also Polytheism of values, Disenchantment of the world, Fideism.

Born once and born twice. William James takes this distinction from Francis Newman in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), where it separates two religious types: the healthy-minded, who live in a spontaneous optimism without awareness of evil, and the sick souls, who have passed through melancholy, the sense of sin or of absurdity, and have found peace only at the price of a second birth, conversion. James invites his audience to turn away from the sky-blue optimistic gospel of the former and listen to the latter, whose experience goes further. The essay uses it to classify its own authors: Ivan Karamazov is the sick soul par excellence, Comte and Renan are once-born. The typology also recalls that James defines religion by the experience of individuals in their solitude, in contrast to Durkheim, in an attested dialogue. See also Oceanic feeling, Static religion and dynamic religion, Ethics of belief.

The mystery that makes one tremble. In The Idea of the Holy (Das Heilige, 1917), Rudolf Otto describes the numinous by its effects in the soul and brings them together in a formula that has become classic: the mysterium tremendum, to which is added the fascinans, what attracts and enraptures. The divine is at once terrifying and fascinating, it repels and it attracts; above all it is the wholly other, ganz Andere, what belongs to no category of the world. The tremendum includes dread, the majesty before which the creature feels itself dust, and the energy of a living power; the fascinans, sweetness, grace, promised bliss. The essay uses this analysis to situate the oceanic feeling of Rolland and of Comte-Sponville: a numinous without tremendum, a pure fascinans. Levinas answers Otto directly, in A Religion for Adults, that the sacred that envelops and transports me is a violence, and that the mysterium tremendum, far from being the heart of religion, is what true religion must free itself from. See also Numinous, Oceanic feeling, The sacred.

Die allgemein menschliche Zwangsneurose. In The Future of an Illusion (1927), Freud compares religious rites to the ceremonials of obsessional neurotics, as he had done as early as 1907, and makes religion the universal obsessional neurosis of humanity, arising like the child's from the Oedipus complex, from the relation to the father. Humanity would pass through a neurotic phase analogous to that of individual childhood, and could leave it through education to reality, as the neurotic does through analysis. The essay stresses the difference from Feuerbach: where Feuerbach saw in God the projected essence of man, to be reappropriated, Freud sees the father of childhood, enlarged, from whom human helplessness asks protection; man writ large against man writ small. It also notes the limit Freud sets himself: religion is an illusion, defined by the wish that commands it and not by its falsity, and the science that is to replace it, our god Logos, is admitted to be not very almighty. Jung will answer that the religious disposition is not merely infantile. See also Illusion, God Logos, Projection.

Unser Gott Λόγος. At the end of The Future of an Illusion (1927), answering the objection of an imaginary interlocutor, Freud grants that science will not replace everything religion gave, but entrusts himself to reason and experience: our god Logos will fulfil those of our wishes that external nature allows, slowly, in an unforeseeable future, for a new humanity; he is not very almighty, and the voice of the intellect is soft but does not rest until it has gained a hearing. Freud borrows the figure from Multatuli, who made Logos and Ananke, necessity, the two divinities of the scholar. The essay notes the weight of the admission: the man who most resolutely wanted to refute the essay's thesis states it himself, by giving reason the name and the place of a god. It also turns § 344 of The Gay Science against the sentence that follows, our science is not an illusion: for Nietzsche, faith in truth is still a faith. The conclusion ranks the god Logos among the transfers of the sacred, beside Durkheim's Society and Stirner's Ego. See also Illusion, Will to truth, Logos.

In The Two Sources of Morality and Religion (1932), the faculty by which the mind produces phantasmal representations, gods, spirits, presences, capable of counterbalancing intelligence. Intelligence, as it developed, endangered the individual and society: it discovers death, it calculates the uncertainty of action, it makes reflective selfishness possible. Nature had at the same time to produce a counterweight, and this counterweight is the religious fables: religion is a defensive reaction of nature against the dissolving power of intelligence, and it is the raison d'être of the fabulating function before that function serves the novel or the theatre. This accounts for static religion, coextensive with our species, which attaches man to life and the individual to society. The essay makes it one of the answers to the question of why people believe, alongside fear, desire and society, and notes that Bergson thereby answers Freud, whom he does not cite: fabulation is indeed a defence, but it does not exhaust the religious, whose highest source is mysticism. See also Static religion and dynamic religion, Illusion, Minimally counterintuitive concepts.

Survivals. In Primitive Culture (1871), Edward Tylor uses the term for the customs, beliefs and practices that persist in a society after the conditions that gave rise to them have disappeared, and that bear witness to an earlier state of culture: superstitions, games, proverbs, rites whose meaning has been forgotten. Animism, a primitive philosophy that explains the world by souls and spirits, is for him a reasonable error, and its remains live on in modern societies as harmful superstition, which ethnography has the office of exposing and marking out for destruction: the science of culture is essentially a reformer's science. The essay ranks Tylor and Frazer in the regime of error in its evolutionist form, which explains the birth of beliefs and not their persistence, and recalls the refutations by Durkheim, for whom a universal and daily illusion would not be one, by Wittgenstein, for whom Frazer is more savage than his savages, and by Malinowski. The essay uses the word, about Nietzsche, in another sense: Schopenhauer's pity as the subtlest survival of Christianity. See also Animism, Eight regimes of critique, Disenchantment of the world.

The two central notions of Jung's psychology after his break with Freud. Archetypes are empty forms of the collective unconscious, filled by the particular representations of each culture, and found with striking constancy in the myths, dreams, visions and delusions of the most distant peoples and ages: the mother, the shadow, the wise old man, and above all the Self, image of psychic totality, which Jung recognizes in Christ, the Buddha, the mandala and the philosopher's stone. Individuation is the process by which the individual enters into relation with this totality; Jung sees in it the psychological equivalent of what religions called salvation, and defines religion, in Psychology and Religion (1938), as the careful observation of the numinosum. The essay follows Buber's objection: psychologism, since God is now only an image of the soul, and gnosis, since the encounter with an external Thou is replaced by knowledge of an inner content. It concludes that Jung makes religion necessary without making it true, and that a religion of the unconscious offers no criterion for refusing the sacrifice an awakened archetype might demand, like Wotan in 1936. See also Numinous, Gnosis, Need and disposition.

fr: Système héroïque et terror management theory
terme: Hero system and terror management theory
definition: From The Denial of Death (1973), which it paraphrases for lack of having consulted the original text, the essay takes from Ernest Becker the following thesis: man knows that he dies, this terror is unbearable, and he covers it over with a causa sui project, the effort to be his own cause, and with heroism, the conviction of having a worth that outlasts death. Every culture is then a hero system, a set of roles, narratives and rites that lets each person believe himself important beyond his disappearance, and religion is the vastest of these systems. Escape from Evil (1975) adds that heroism needs victims. Greenberg, Solomon and Pyszczynski drew from it, from 1986 onwards, terror management theory: being reminded of death should strengthen attachment to one's worldview and hostility to others; the essay notes that the effect was not replicated by Many Labs 4 in 2022. It draws from Becker that the refoundations are replacement hero systems, and objects that he confuses the need for meaning, which is universal, with the need for immortality. See also Need and disposition, Scapegoat mechanism, Illusion.

The Sacred Canopy (1967), the book in which Peter Berger applies the theory of the social construction of reality to religion. Every society is an enterprise of world-building, and this world, which he calls by a Greek word, nomos, is an order of meanings that shields human beings from chaos; the individual torn from it, by bereavement, exile or catastrophe, becomes anomic, worldless. Religion is the sacred canopy stretched over this nomos, which grounds it by relating it to a cosmic order, and its first function is not happiness but meaning, as is shown by theodicy, which makes suffering bearable by explaining it. The canopy holds through plausibility structures: a religion is believed only if one's surroundings take it as self-evident, and modern pluralism, which brings everyone face to face with other beliefs, undermines this self-evidence; a chosen belief does not have the same authority as a world. Berger had drawn from this a prediction of secularization that he retracted in 1999, the world having remained as furiously religious as ever. The essay distinguishes the shelter of meaning, which does not disappear, from the institution, which can recede. See also Invisible religion, Secularization, Theodicy.

The Invisible Religion (1967), a revised version of a German book of 1963, in which Thomas Luckmann proposes a reading of modernity different from Berger's. He starts from a very broad definition: religious is everything by which the human organism transcends its biological nature and gives itself a world of meaning. In modern societies this function is no longer performed by the Churches, whose influence is receding, but by private systems of meaning, assembled by each person from available themes, self-realization, the family, sexuality, mobility, and which form an invisible religion, without institution or dogma. Secularization is therefore not the disappearance of religion but its privatization. The essay judges this reading subtler and closer to the spiritualities without God of its Part Twelve, but it marks its limit: a definition that encompasses everything no longer makes it possible to distinguish what the sacrifice criterion seeks to distinguish, and that is why it separates two terms, the shelter of meaning, which does not disappear, and the institution, which can recede. Hervieu-Léger will extend the analysis with the pilgrim and the convert. See also Sacred canopy, Secularization, Believing lineage.
